newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian election overshadowed by crisis, violence.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian election overshadowed by crisis, violence.

text.p: Bulgarians looked set to deliver a sharp rebuff to their ruling ex-communists on Sunday as they went to the polls under the shadow of economic crisis and rising political violence.
Shortly after voting in the presidential election began, police scrambled to a city centre school where President Zhelyu Zhelev was due to cast his ballot, after a caller telephoned a bomb threat.
A thorough search found nothing, state radio said.
Nerves of polling officials have been on edge since Wednesday when a crude bomb destroyed the car of Haralambi Anchev, a member of the Central Electoral Committee.

Many voters said they blamed the ruling Socialist party for soaring prices and opinion polls predict a comfortable win for opposition candidate Petar Stoyanov over Socialist Culture Minister Ivan Marazov.

"All my life I have voted for our people, the communists, now the socialists. This time I voted for Stoyanov because things have to improve," said a 62-year-old National Security Service officer in Sofia's wealthy Lozenets district.
Stoyanov won 43.9 percent in a first round of voting last weekend, comfortably ahead of Marazov but short of the 50 percent he needed to win outright.

Campaigning for Bulgaria's second presidential election since the end of communist rule in 1989 has been marred by bombings and violence culminating in the October 2 assassination of former prime minister Andrei Lukanov.
Voting also coincides with an International Monetary Fund mission discussing terms for release of a $115 million credit vital to prevent Bulgaria defaulting on its foreign debt.

"I am going to vote for Stoyanov, although I am not enchanted with the opposition either, but this is my only way to protest against what is happening now in the country," said a 50-year old engineer.
Electoral officials said early turnout appeared lower than for last week's first round.

Under Bulgaria's post-communist constitution the president is a largely ceremonial figure and real power lies with parliament where Prime Minister Zhan Videnov's divided Bulgarian Socialist Party has a majority.
But several voters said they hoped the presidential election would force early parliamentary polls. "We need changes in all the institutions," said technician Plomen Parvanov, 33.
Opinion polls give Stoyanov between 57 and 64 percent of the vote this time, well ahead of his rival.
Neighbouring Romania and Yugoslavia, also voting on Sunday, are themselves battling economic crisis but reform laggard Bulgaria has the lowest foreign investment in the region.
Union of Democratic Forces candidate Stoyanov is an advocate of a market economy and closer ties with the European Union and NATO.

The maverick populist head of the Bulgarian Business Bloc, George Ganchev, won the lion's share of protest votes last week, polling 21.8 percent, but he has declined to back either second round candidate.
